subject: ICT
intro: Seven original 40-minute GROW lessons adapted from the uploaded ICT sequence. Pupils practise real software skills using fictional club tasks and supplied offline starter files. Source references to NC Computing, Functional Skills, AQA UAS and ProjectEVOLVE are provisional planning labels only; no accreditation, qualification evidence or verified full-framework alignment is claimed. Use school-approved software and storage with accessible support. Do not collect passwords, personal online histories, pupil data or public posts. No lesson requires sending or publishing anything.

sources.title: Uploaded GROW ICT Autumn 1 materials, Weeks 1–7
sources.note: All seven original PPTX and seven matching DOCX were read; exact filenames are listed per lesson. The sequence is preserved: real task, word processing, file organisation, presentation, data, online risk/footprint, digital identity project. References to NC Computing, Functional Skills, AQA UAS and ProjectEVOLVE are unverified planning labels only. No endorsement, full alignment, award banking or accredited assessment is claimed.

Core tasks require no personal survey, online account, sending, publishing or public presentation.

sources.note: Primary UK guidance supports recognising pressure/authority tactics, not relying on appearance/spelling alone, pausing and checking via a known official route rather than the suspicious message. The lesson uses inert fictional examples, without active links or credential entry. Checked 7 September 2026.

sources.note: Primary UK educational guidance supports voluntary participation, reducing identifying information, recognising possible copies/sharing and seeking support. The pack does not recommend joining a platform or reproduce potentially changeable platform age examples. Checked 7 September 2026.

sources.note: CEOP’s remit is online sexual abuse and grooming; it is not a general route for every bullying, fake-account or hacking problem. School adults help match the concern to the appropriate route. Verified earlier in this session on 7 September 2026.

lessons.title: Log on and complete a real task
lessons.big_question: How do I complete a useful digital task and check it is saved?
lessons.objective: Access the approved workspace, choose a suitable tool, complete a short club plan and save/reopen it safely.
success: I can access the approved task without sharing login details.
I can choose a suitable tool and complete a useful three-step plan.
I can save, reopen and check my work, asking for support when needed.

vocabulary.meaning: A program used to carry out a task.
Software for creating and editing written documents.
Store a file’s changes in a chosen location.
Open a saved file again to check it.

slides.title: Log on and complete a real task
body: Today: make a short plan that a fictional Makers Club member could follow.
We will open, do, save and check. Using support is allowed.
slides.prompt: What would tell us the whole task is finished?
slides.answer: The plan is useful and accurate, and the saved file can be found and reopened.
slides.notes: Adapted from uploaded GROW ICT Week 1 deck and record. NC Computing and AQA UAS labels are provisional source references only. Replaces public mood checks, required personal details and “try two fixes before help”.

slides.title: Start with an approved workspace
body: Use the school’s usual login route. Keep passwords and codes off worksheets, photographs and shared screens.
If access fails or a prompt seems unusual, pause and ask an adult.
Adjust the display or input method so you can work comfortably.
slides.prompt: Should you tell a partner your password so they can help?
slides.answer: No. Ask an adult to support the approved login process without sharing secret details.
slides.notes: Do not demonstrate a real password on the projector. Adult verifies that the pupil reached the approved workspace, not the credential used. No repeated trial-and-error sign-ins.

slides.title: Choose the tool for the purpose
body: A short written session plan needs a word processor.
A set of slides needs presentation software.
A table that calculates vote totals needs a spreadsheet.
slides.prompt: Which tool fits today’s three-step plan, and why?
slides.answer: A word processor can create and edit clear written instructions.
slides.notes: Use Word, Writer or the school-managed equivalent. No exact toolbar positions are assumed. Browser/email examples are discussion only, not sending or live research tasks.

slides.title: Our real task: a usable club plan
body: The club helper needs three steps: read the task card; draw two ideas; choose one and explain it.
Open GROW_W1_Session_Plan_Starter.docx from the supplied starter folder.
The details are fictional; the editing and saving skills are real.
slides.prompt: What must the helper be able to understand?
slides.answer: The order of the three actions and what to do at each step.
slides.notes: If a learner cannot open DOCX locally, use a teacher-approved native copy or recreate the supplied text in a blank word processor. Do not penalise a compatibility problem.

slides.title: We do: edit one line
body: Select the first placeholder only. Replace it with: “First: read the task card.”
Check that the title and other lines are still present.
If an accidental edit happens, use Undo or ask for help before continuing.
slides.prompt: Why check the page after replacing text?
slides.answer: Selecting too much can replace other content; checking catches an unintended change early.
slides.notes: Model selection slowly, then read back. Offer keyboard, mouse, touch or accessible input according to the pupil’s setup. Do not assume a shortcut works identically on every device.

slides.title: You do: finish the useful text
body: Next: draw two design ideas.
Finally: choose one idea and explain the choice.
Read the three steps in order; check capitals, spaces and full stops.
slides.prompt: Can someone follow the plan without asking what “do it” means?
slides.answer: Yes, if each step names a clear action and the order is explicit.
slides.notes: Adults may scribe planning ideas, but observe the digital operation the pupil actually performs. Distinguish a completed template from independently demonstrated skills.

slides.title: Save a copy you can find
body: Use the approved save/copy route. Name the file GROW_W1_Club_Plan_v1.docx.
Choose the school-approved working folder and check its displayed location.
Save changes, then reopen the saved copy and read the final line.
slides.prompt: Is seeing a file name enough to prove the last edit was saved?
slides.answer: No. Reopening and checking the final line gives better evidence that the intended version was saved.
slides.notes: Teacher may approve a native-format extension. Record only the task folder’s safe label, never a full path containing personal account details. Explain local saving versus managed cloud behaviour for this setup.

slides.title: A sensible pause can prevent a problem
body: A window is hidden: check the open apps before opening another copy.
A login fails: ask an adult through the school route.
A strange download or permission request appears: stop and check.
slides.prompt: Which problem is safe to investigate with an open-app check?
slides.answer: A hidden window. Do not experiment with credentials, permissions or unknown downloads.
slides.notes: A safe check is an option, not an entry requirement for help. Do not close an app without considering unsaved work or restart a device during the task without adult support.

slides.title: Your practical record
body: Task 1: explain the tool choice.
Task 2: complete the three-step file and save it.
Task 3: reopen, check and record a next step.
slides.prompt: Which evidence shows a completed digital action?
slides.answer: The reopened file and a demonstration of the action, with the support used recorded.
slides.notes: Support: edit one line with a model. Standard: complete/save/reopen all three. Stretch: improve an unclear instruction and explain why it is better.

slides.title: Show the whole job
body: Point to the title and the final line in your reopened saved copy.
Name one place you can get help if access or saving is unclear.
slides.prompt: What will you do before leaving the device?
slides.answer: Check saving, close the task safely and lock or sign out according to the school routine.
slides.notes: Do not collect passwords or screenshots of login screens. Finish with an accessible transition and adult assistance where needed.

worksheet.title: Log on and complete a real task — practical record

tasks.heading: 1 · Choose a useful tool
tasks.prompt: The fictional club helper needs three written steps. Choose a tool and explain why.
items: Choices: word processor · presentation software · spreadsheet.
A useful plan should tell the helper: first ___; next ___; finally ___.
tasks.answer: Word processor: it is suited to written instructions. First read the task card; next draw two ideas; finally choose one and explain the choice.

tasks.heading: 2 · Complete the real digital task
tasks.prompt: Open GROW_W1_Session_Plan_Starter.docx. Replace its three placeholder lines with the complete plan below, then save a copy in the approved working folder.
items: First: read the task card.
Next: draw two design ideas.
Finally: choose one idea and explain the choice.
Output: GROW_W1_Club_Plan_v1.docx, or the same base name in the teacher-approved native format.
tasks.answer: The saved file contains the title and all three accurate ordered instructions. Record the support used for selecting/replacing text and saving; do not infer independence from the finished page.

tasks.heading: 3 · Reopen and check
tasks.prompt: Reopen the saved copy. Read the final instruction and record what you checked. Use the fictional issue if no problem occurred.
items: The line I found was: ___. One check I made: ___.
Fictional issue: the document window seems to have disappeared but the app is still open. What could you safely check?
My next practice step: ___. Do not write usernames, passwords or account paths.
tasks.answer: Final line should tell the helper to choose one idea and explain the choice. Check open apps for the hidden window; ask for support at any point. Suitable next step: practise selecting one line or locating the saved task file.

worksheet.exit_question: Why reopen a saved file before calling the task complete?
worksheet.exit_answer: To check the intended copy is findable and contains the latest changes.

preparation: Check approved login, word processor and storage before the lesson; distribute a writable copy of the starter.
Make the safe task folder location visible using a generic label.
Prepare accessible input, larger display text and an adult help route.
materials: Printed plan/check cards and practical record

timing.activity: Access the approved workspace and settle
Match tool to purpose and read the brief
Model selection, editing and saving
Complete the plan and save a copy
Reopen and record the checks
Discuss a safe problem response and exit evidence
Close/lock or sign out and reset

teacher.modelling: Model one placeholder replacement, read it back, save a named copy to the agreed task folder and reopen it. Narrate only visible task choices; never display real login secrets. Explain why a hidden window is different from a lost saved file.
misconceptions: Independence can include using a checklist and asking for appropriate help.
A file name alone does not prove the last change was saved.
A hidden window is not necessarily lost work.
Troubleshooting must stay within authorised classroom actions.
teacher.support: Offer a one-line model, read the task aloud and provide selected-text practice. Let the learner choose keyboard, touch, mouse or accessible input. Record which operations they demonstrate and what support is used.
teacher.stretch: Ask the pupil to replace an unclear instruction such as “do the next bit” with a usable step, then explain how saving a copy protects the supplied starter.
teacher.fallback: Use the full printed brief to arrange the three instruction cards and select the correct software card. Adult can demonstrate the save/reopen process. Record this as planning/understanding evidence; digital operation remains to be observed later.
teacher.safeguarding: Use only school-approved accounts and task folders. Never request or record passwords, security codes, personal account names or login screenshots. Do not send the plan, make an account or change device permissions. Stop unusual prompts and involve staff.
teacher.assessment: Observe tool choice, one edit, the named save location and successful reopening of the intended copy. Use “demonstrated with model”, “with prompt” or “independently” descriptively. Paper planning does not certify practical competence.

resources.title: Task and safe-check cards
resources.instructions: Use the full brief to make the plan. Read each check separately; the cards contain no real account information.
items: Brief · A fictional Makers Club helper needs three ordered instructions for a design activity. The plan will be kept as a local classroom file.
Step 1 · First: read the task card.
Step 2 · Next: draw two design ideas.
Step 3 · Finally: choose one idea and explain the choice.
Tool card · Word processor: written documents. Presentation software: slides. Spreadsheet: tables, calculations and charts.
Check A · Has the saved copy kept the title and all three steps?
Check B · Can you reopen the file and read the final instruction?
Safe pause · If login, downloads or permissions are unclear, stop and ask an adult. A hidden window can be checked in the open apps. No “two fixes” rule blocks help.
answers: The intended tool is a word processor. The three step cards give the complete expected task content.
Reopening the correct named copy and checking its text is the practical completion check. Lock or sign out using the school routine after saving.

lessons.title: Format a notice for its reader
lessons.big_question: How can layout and careful checking make a notice easier to use?
lessons.objective: Edit and format a fictional club notice with purposeful headings, readable text and a checked final copy.
success: I can use formatting to make important information easier to find.
I can correct wording by reading as well as using spellcheck.
I can explain a useful change and save/reopen the final copy.

vocabulary.meaning: Changing how text is presented.
A short label showing what a section is about.
How text is positioned across a line.
Read carefully to check meaning and mistakes.

slides.title: Format a notice for its reader
body: Today: repair a tiny, crowded notice for a fictional Makers Club.
The message should be accurate and easy to find, not simply colourful.
slides.prompt: What information should a reader find quickly?
slides.answer: What the club is, when/where the fictional event happens, what to bring and how to request support.
slides.notes: Adapted from Week 2 word-processing deck and record. Functional Skills/AQA UAS labels are unverified planning references. Provides the missing messy source document and purposeful, attainable editing criteria.

slides.title: The reader has a job to do
body: The notice contains the right kind of information, but it is one crowded paragraph in tiny text.
It also says “meat” where it should say “meet”, and misspells “library”.
A spellchecker might miss a real word used in the wrong place.
slides.prompt: Why is making the title bigger not enough?
slides.answer: The wording still needs checking and the information needs useful groups or paragraphs.
slides.notes: Open GROW_W2_Notice_Messy.docx. Its 8-point text is deliberately poor; enlarge the view for access while pupils work. Do not make tiny print an unavoidable reading barrier.

slides.title: Format with a reason
body: Use a meaningful heading and readable body text. Keep text dark on a light background.
Use left-aligned paragraphs for the details; bold can highlight key choices.
Avoid using colour alone to tell the reader what matters.
slides.prompt: Which words might need emphasis: every word, or the activity choices?
slides.answer: The activity choices: drawing, model making and planning. Too much emphasis hides the useful differences.
slides.notes: The suggested 18–22-point heading and 12–14-point body are starting points for a printed notice, adjustable for need. They are classroom design choices, not universal compliance claims.

slides.title: We do: a useful heading
body: Replace the opening words with the heading “Makers Club pop-up”.
Place the event details in their own paragraph.
Keep the three activity choices together so a reader can compare them.
slides.prompt: What changed for the reader?
slides.answer: The heading names the notice, and grouped details are easier to find.
slides.notes: Show selection before applying formatting so the learner can see what the tool affects. Use the equivalent formatting controls in the available software; menu positions vary.

slides.title: Check the word, then the meaning
body: “librery” should be “library”. A spelling suggestion may help.
“The group will meat” should be “The group will meet”. Both words exist.
Read each sentence after making a change; do not accept every suggestion automatically.
slides.prompt: Which correction needs attention to meaning?
slides.answer: Meat → meet. The sentence is about gathering, not food.
slides.notes: If the application offers no suggestion, the printed correction examples still support the reasoning task. Do not require pupils to invent a rejected spellcheck suggestion.

slides.title: You do: make the notice usable
body: Open GROW_W2_Notice_Messy.docx and save a working copy.
Add a heading, readable paragraphs and bold the three activity choices.
Correct capitals, “librery” and “meat”; keep the fictional details accurate.
slides.prompt: What should remain true after formatting?
slides.answer: Thursday at 15:15, library, bring a pencil, activity choices and an option for quiet written ideas/support.
slides.notes: Provide the complete correct content in the resource sheet; copying accurately with support is valid. There is no email, print distribution or live event invitation.

slides.title: Which change helps?
body: A: use six fonts and make every sentence bold.
B: use a clear heading, consistent body text and spaced paragraphs.
C: replace small body text with readable text, then proofread.
slides.prompt: Which choices make the notice more useful?
slides.answer: B and C. The improvement should help readers find and understand accurate information.
slides.notes: Discuss design in relation to purpose, not personal taste or a rigid “professional look”. Avoid grades based on decorative skill.

slides.title: Run the finishing check
body: Read the text. Check heading, fictional time/place and spelling in context.
Save as GROW_W2_Club_Notice_v1.docx in the approved task folder.
Reopen the copy and confirm the heading and last support sentence are present.
slides.prompt: What will you check if reopening shows the old tiny text?
slides.answer: Check whether the correct copy/version and save location were used; ask for help without overwriting the starter.
slides.notes: A teacher-approved native-format extension is acceptable. Check any conversion warning with staff. Do not imply that closing without saving is harmless.

slides.title: Your practical record
body: Task 1: identify a reader problem and plan a change.
Task 2: edit and format the digital notice.
Task 3: explain a wording correction and verify the saved result.
slides.prompt: What counts as evidence beyond ticking a checklist?
slides.answer: Show the heading, paragraph structure and corrected wording in the reopened file.
slides.notes: Support: use a paragraph-by-paragraph model. Standard: apply purposeful changes and explain one. Stretch: justify a design choice and identify a real-word mistake spellcheck may miss.

slides.title: Meaning and layout work together
body: Complete: “I changed ___ so the reader can ___.”
Point to the corresponding change in your saved file.
slides.prompt: Give one specific example.
slides.answer: I put the event details in a separate paragraph so the reader can find the fictional time and place.
slides.notes: Use a private adult check or written/pointed response. No compulsory peer performance or disclosure is needed.

worksheet.title: Format a notice for its reader — practical record

tasks.heading: 1 · Read like the audience
tasks.prompt: The starter notice is tiny and crowded. Identify a problem and a purposeful change.
items: The reader needs the club name, fictional time/place, choices, what to bring and support option.
Problem: ___. Change: ___. This helps because ___.
tasks.answer: Example: the details are one long paragraph; separate event details, choices and support information so the reader can scan them.

tasks.heading: 2 · Edit the notice
tasks.prompt: Open GROW_W2_Notice_Messy.docx. Save a copy, then use the complete resource text to improve it.
items: Add “Makers Club pop-up” as a heading. Use readable body text and left-aligned paragraphs.
Bold drawing, model making and planning. Keep Thursday, 15:15 and library accurate.
Correct “librery” and the sentence containing “meat”.
Save as GROW_W2_Club_Notice_v1.docx, or the approved native format.
tasks.answer: The correct notice is supplied on the resource sheet. Evidence should show purposeful formatting and accurate wording, not merely use of every toolbar button.

tasks.heading: 3 · Check and explain
tasks.prompt: Reopen the saved copy. Check both the appearance and meaning.
items: One formatting change that helps the reader: ___.
“The group will meat near the librery desk.” Correct both errors: ___.
Why might spellcheck miss one of these? ___.
I reopened and checked: ___.
tasks.answer: Correct sentence: “The group will meet near the library desk.” Meat is a correctly spelled word used with the wrong meaning, so spellcheck may miss it. Reopen and show the revised heading and support sentence.

worksheet.exit_question: Why should we read the sentence even after using spellcheck?
worksheet.exit_answer: A correctly spelled word can still be wrong in context, such as meat instead of meet.

preparation: Open the deliberately messy starter on the available word processor and confirm it is writable.
Provide enlarged viewing/text or the printed readable source for pupils who cannot access 8-point starter text.
Locate the local formatting, proofreading and save-copy controls; do not assume a particular toolbar layout.
materials: Complete correct notice and proofreading cards

timing.activity: Access starter and read the brief
Identify reader needs and plan changes
Model heading, selection and two wording corrections
Edit, format and save the notice
Reopen and check accuracy with the record
Explain one purposeful change and exit
Save/close and reset

teacher.modelling: Change one heading and paragraph while narrating its purpose. Correct “librery”, then read the sentence containing “meat” to show that proofreading also checks meaning. Save a working copy and keep the original starter available.
misconceptions: More colours and fonts do not necessarily improve access.
Every sentence in bold removes useful emphasis.
Spellcheck is not a guarantee of correct meaning.
A format choice should serve a reader need.
teacher.support: Provide the correct notice in short chunks and model one selected-text operation. Accept copying from the resource or dictated wording while observing the pupil’s actual edits. Enlarged text and keyboard support are available.
teacher.stretch: Ask the pupil to compare two justified layout choices and identify what a spellchecker cannot establish about the event details. They can improve the support sentence’s prominence without changing its meaning.
teacher.fallback: On paper, arrange the printed notice sections in a logical order and mark a heading/keywords. Correct the two wording errors. This demonstrates editing decisions; revisit actual software use when equipment is available.
teacher.safeguarding: The notice is fictional and stays in the approved task folder. Do not add pupil names, email addresses or real contact details. Nothing is emailed, posted or publicly distributed. Check save/format warnings with staff.
teacher.assessment: Observe selection/formatting, grouped accurate content, two corrected errors and a reopened final file. Ask for one reason linked to readability. A ticked feature list alone is insufficient evidence of purposeful editing.

resources.title: Complete notice and proofreading cards
resources.instructions: Use this correct text as the source for your edited notice. Separate the sections into readable paragraphs; the event is fictional.
items: Heading · Makers Club pop-up
Event details · Come to our fictional Makers Club on Thursday at 15:15 in the library. The group will meet near the library desk.
Choices · Choose drawing, model making or planning. Bring a pencil.
Access and support · A quiet written-idea option is available. Ask the club adult if you would like support.
Proofreading card A · librery → library.
Proofreading card B · The group will meat near the desk. “Meat” is a real word, but the intended word is “meet”.
Design check · Meaningful heading; readable dark text; left-aligned body; useful paragraph breaks; emphasis on three choices.
Saved-file check · Reopen the intended copy. Confirm the heading, Thursday 15:15/library details and final support sentence.
answers: The four content cards contain all required wording. Accept equivalent accurate sentences with the same information.
The “meat” example shows why reading for meaning is still needed. A pupil can explain this without an actual spellcheck rejection appearing.

lessons.title: Save, organise and find your files
lessons.big_question: How can a file name and location help me find the right version?
lessons.objective: Organise supplied practice copies using meaningful names and folders, then retrieve and check the intended version.
success: I can choose a file name that describes its contents and version.
I can organise practice copies into suitable folders.
I can find the right file again and explain its storage location.

vocabulary.meaning: A saved piece of digital work.
A container used to organise files.
A particular saved stage of a file.
Where a file is stored.

slides.title: Save, organise and find your files
body: Today: organise a disposable practice folder and find the right version again.
Only use the supplied copies. The task is about reliable finding, not a speed race.
slides.prompt: What makes “Document1” hard to find later?
slides.answer: It gives little information about the subject, contents or stage of the work.
slides.notes: Adapted from Week 3 file-management deck and record. Replaces a timed race and broad changes to pupils’ existing folders with a safe self-contained practice folder.

slides.title: Three files need clearer names
body: Document1.txt contains a Makers Club session plan.
notes.txt contains garden design notes.
Untitled2.txt contains Makers Club facts.
slides.prompt: Suggest a useful name for the club plan.
slides.answer: Club_Plan_v1.txt: it names the content and version.
slides.notes: Read the provided plain-text files. Explain that the extension identifies a file type; changing it is not a conversion. If extensions are hidden, leave that setting as configured.

slides.title: Name, location and version work together
body: Use a meaningful base name, such as Club_Plan, plus v1 for the first saved stage.
Use ICT for the club plan/facts and Design for the garden notes in this exercise.
Keep a later draft as a new version when you need to preserve the earlier one.
slides.prompt: Would “final_final_reallyfinal” be a clear version plan?
slides.answer: No. A simple consistent stage or version label is easier to compare.
slides.notes: The folder mapping is an exercise convention; other sensible mappings are possible if justified. Do not imply only one organisation scheme is universally correct.

slides.title: We do: organise a practice copy
body: Work inside your supplied GROW_W3_File_Practice copy. Create ICT and Design folders.
Copy Document1.txt from Inbox into ICT, then rename the copy Club_Plan_v1.txt.
Open it and check that the contents match the name.
slides.prompt: Why check the contents instead of trusting a name?
slides.answer: A file can be renamed incorrectly. Opening it confirms that it is the plan.
slides.notes: Teacher distributes an individual writable copy. Copy creates an additional file; move changes its location. This activity preserves Inbox originals for recovery.

slides.title: You do: give each copy a home
body: Copy notes.txt into Design and name it Garden_Notes_v1.txt.
Copy Untitled2.txt into ICT and name it Club_Facts_v1.txt.
Check that the three names describe what is inside.
slides.prompt: Which file belongs in Design in our agreed plan?
slides.answer: Garden_Notes_v1.txt, because it contains the garden design notes.
slides.notes: Allow accessible copy/paste or equivalent controls; do not require drag-and-drop dexterity. Never tidy unrelated shared or personal folders.

slides.title: A second version keeps an earlier stage
body: Make a copy of Club_Plan_v1.txt called Club_Plan_v2.txt inside ICT.
Add “Check: explain why the chosen design could work.” to v2, then save it.
Open v1 and v2 to check which one contains the new line.
slides.prompt: What should remain in v1?
slides.answer: The original three-step plan without the added Check line.
slides.notes: Pupils can use the editor’s save-copy route or duplicate then edit. Model how to confirm the file name before an edit so the wrong version is not overwritten.

slides.title: Where does the work live?
body: A file may be on the device, a school network drive or managed cloud storage.
A folder called Documents does not by itself tell you which of these applies.
Ask about the approved location and check saving/sync status for your setup.
slides.prompt: Does a cloud file always mean the latest edit is available everywhere?
slides.answer: No. Connection, sync status, permissions and the version opened can affect access.
slides.notes: Do not promise cloud access on every device or imply local files are never backed up. Staff should explain the actual managed arrangement and recovery route.

slides.title: Find the intended version
body: Close the practice files after saving. Find ICT, then Club_Plan_v2.txt.
You may browse the folder or search by its name. Recent files can be a starting point.
Check the version name and the added Check line.
slides.prompt: Why might opening the first recent file be insufficient?
slides.answer: It might be v1 or another copy. Check location, version and content.
slides.notes: No timer or speed score is required. Observe the chosen retrieval strategy and provide a prompt route if needed.

slides.title: Your practical record
body: Task 1: plan meaningful names and folders.
Task 2: organise copies and preserve two plan versions.
Task 3: retrieve v2 and explain where it is stored.
slides.prompt: What evidence shows the correct version was found?
slides.answer: The file is in the intended ICT folder, named v2, and includes the new Check line.
slides.notes: Support: organise one file with a model and compare two versions. Standard: complete all copies. Stretch: explain copy versus move and a risk of ambiguous version names.

slides.title: Reliable beats rushed
body: Show where you would look for the latest practice plan.
Explain one habit that would help if work is hard to find.
slides.prompt: Give a helpful habit.
slides.answer: Use consistent names, record the approved folder, save/check versions and ask for support when unsure.
slides.notes: Losing work is not automatically a pupil’s fault. Faults, access and synchronisation may need staff help. End with safe saving and closing.

worksheet.title: Save, organise and find your files — practical record

tasks.heading: 1 · Plan names and folders
tasks.prompt: Use the supplied file contents to choose meaningful names. Work only inside the practice copy.
items: Document1.txt = club session plan → ICT / Club_Plan_v1.txt.
notes.txt = garden design notes → Design / Garden_Notes_v1.txt.
Untitled2.txt = club facts → ICT / Club_Facts_v1.txt.
Why does one new name help? ___.
tasks.answer: Names tell the reader the content and version. The given folder plan separates this exercise’s ICT and design work. Do not alter a file extension to change its type.

tasks.heading: 2 · Organise and version the copies
tasks.prompt: In your writable GROW_W3_File_Practice copy, create ICT and Design folders. Copy the three Inbox files into their planned locations and rename the copies.
items: Keep the Inbox originals for recovery.
Create ICT / Club_Plan_v2.txt as a new copy of v1.
Add only to v2: “Check: explain why the chosen design could work.” Save it.
Compare v1 and v2. Which has the new line? ___.
tasks.answer: The three copied files have the stated names/locations. v2 contains the added Check line; v1 retains the original plan. Staff records the actual copy/rename/edit operations demonstrated.

tasks.heading: 3 · Find and verify
tasks.prompt: Close saved files, then retrieve the intended v2 copy without a race.
items: My route: browse folders / search name / recent file followed by checks.
The name and final line I checked: ___.
The approved storage is on this device / school network / managed cloud / I need to ask.
Why might the first Recent result be the wrong copy? ___.
tasks.answer: Find ICT / Club_Plan_v2.txt and confirm the Check line. A recent result could be v1 or another copy. Correct storage description depends on the actual school setup; “I need to ask” is a useful next action, not evidence of knowing the location.

worksheet.exit_question: What three things help confirm you found the intended file?
worksheet.exit_answer: Its meaningful name/version, the intended folder/location and its expected contents.

preparation: Distribute a writable individual copy of GROW_W3_File_Practice with the three complete Inbox TXT files.
Confirm the actual storage arrangement: device, school network or managed cloud, including any sync indicator.
Keep a master practice folder available for recovery; restrict this activity to copies.
materials: School file manager and simple text editor

timing.activity: Access only the approved practice copy
Model content-based names and folders
Copy and rename the three files
Create/check v2 while preserving v1
Retrieve the correct version and record evidence
Explain storage and a sensible recovery route
Exit check
Save/close and reset

teacher.modelling: Open Document1 before naming it. Create its folder, copy then rename it, and show where the original remains. Duplicate the plan for v2, check the window/file name, add one line and compare both versions.
misconceptions: Recent files is a route, not proof of the correct version.
Changing an extension does not convert a file.
Documents may be redirected or synchronised; its label alone does not show storage type.
Autosave/cloud access should be checked, not assumed.
Finding accurately matters more than a 20-second target.
teacher.support: Use a printed mapping and demonstrate one copy at a time. Keyboard copy/paste, large icons or staff-supported navigation can replace dragging. Observe one successful retrieval without grading speed.
teacher.stretch: Ask the pupil to explain copy versus move, detect a deliberately misnamed practice copy, or design a consistent version rule for future work without altering real existing folders.
teacher.fallback: Use the full printed file cards to sort names into ICT/Design and identify which version has the added line. Mark this as organisation understanding; practical file operations still need observation later.
teacher.safeguarding: Operate only on supplied disposable copies in approved storage. No deletion, system-folder changes, access overrides or cloud-account changes. Do not record full paths containing personal account information. Ask staff about unexpected sync or permission prompts.
teacher.assessment: Observe file content check, useful name, correct destination, preservation of v1 and successful retrieval of v2. Record supports and any operation requiring later practice. Do not treat a fast click sequence as evidence of understanding.

resources.title: File names, folders and version cards
resources.instructions: Use the complete contents below to choose names, destinations and versions. These are practice files, not real personal documents.
items: A · Inbox / Document1.txt: “Makers Club session plan. First: read the task card. Next: draw two design ideas. Finally: choose one idea and explain the choice.”
B · Inbox / notes.txt: “Garden design notes. The fictional garden plan needs a wide path, a quiet seat and space for plants.”
C · Inbox / Untitled2.txt: “Makers Club facts. Members can draw, build or plan. Written ideas and spoken ideas are welcome.”
Destination 1 · ICT: Club_Plan_v1.txt and Club_Facts_v1.txt.
Destination 2 · Design: Garden_Notes_v1.txt.
Version 2 addition · “Check: explain why the chosen design could work.” Add to Club_Plan_v2.txt only.
Retrieve check · Folder/location + meaningful file/version name + expected content.
Storage check · Device, school network and managed cloud are different possibilities. Ask staff which applies; do not guess from the Documents label.
answers: A → ICT / Club_Plan_v1.txt. B → Design / Garden_Notes_v1.txt. C → ICT / Club_Facts_v1.txt.
v2 has the extra Check line; v1 does not. Inbox originals remain for recovery. Reliable retrieval uses name, location and content together.

lessons.title: Build slides that help an audience
lessons.big_question: How can a short deck show useful information clearly?
lessons.objective: Create a four-slide fictional club presentation, insert a supplied factual chart image purposefully and improve the saved deck after checking it.
success: I can organise four slides with a clear purpose and readable text.
I can insert and resize a supplied chart image without distorting it.
I can explain the order and make one useful improvement.

vocabulary.meaning: The people who will use or view the information.
The arrangement of text and visuals.
The relationship between an image’s width and height.
A short explanation placed with a visual.

slides.title: Build slides that help an audience
body: Today: introduce a fictional Makers Club in four clear slides.
Use the supplied facts and chart; no personal photos or online image searches are needed.
slides.prompt: What should the audience understand after four slides?
slides.answer: What the club offers, how people can join in and one accurate fact from the fictional votes.
slides.notes: Adapted from Week 4 presentation deck/record. One relevant supplied chart image replaces a fixed two-picture requirement; choice of private preview replaces compulsory presenting. Source alignment labels remain unverified.

slides.title: Give each slide a job
body: 1: introduce the club. 2: show the activities.
3: explain accessible ways to join. 4: show what the fictional votes say.
Keep key text brief and readable; use one consistent style.
slides.prompt: Why give the slides an order before decorating them?
slides.answer: The order helps the audience follow the information and decide what each slide needs.
slides.notes: Use the four-slide starter. The design goal is clear communication; no fixed five-second reading speed or universal word-count guarantee is claimed.

slides.title: We do: turn facts into useful points
body: Source: “Members can choose drawing, model making, coding or gardening.”
Slide points: “Drawing and model making” and “Coding and gardening”.
The title “Activities to try” explains what the points are for.
slides.prompt: Has the shorter version kept all four options?
slides.answer: Yes. Each option remains, but the information is easier to scan.
slides.notes: Model replacing the starter placeholders, not adding another paragraph underneath them. Do not require learners to type text already present elsewhere.

slides.title: A visual must do a job
body: The supplied chart shows fictional club votes: Drawing 7; Model making 9; Coding 3; Gardening 5.
It can support a takeaway: “Model making received the most votes: 9.”
Label it as fictional data; the chart does not describe our class.
slides.prompt: Why does this chart earn a place on the final slide?
slides.answer: It supports a specific fact about the fictional choices rather than acting only as decoration.
slides.notes: The data is fully supplied before spreadsheet teaching in Week 5. Use assets/GROW_Club_Votes_Chart.png. Avoid claiming a plurality of 9 out of 24 is a majority.

slides.title: Insert and resize with care
body: Use the image-insertion route to choose GROW_Club_Votes_Chart.png from the supplied assets folder.
Keep the width/height proportions linked, or use the appropriate corner handle.
Check the labels remain readable and the chart does not cover text.
slides.prompt: What might stretching only the width do?
slides.answer: It distorts the chart and can make the visual misleading or harder to read.
slides.notes: Demonstrate on the available software. Some handles/platform behaviours differ; check the result rather than promising a modifier key. The chart is original factual artwork from the pack’s fictional dataset.

slides.title: You do: complete the four-slide story
body: Use the source cards to replace every placeholder in GROW_W4_Mini_Deck_Starter.pptx.
Add the chart, a fictional-data caption and one accurate takeaway.
Keep headings, body text and colours consistent enough to read.
slides.prompt: What should not appear in the finished slides?
slides.answer: Unfilled brackets, personal details, distorted chart labels or claims unsupported by the source cards.
slides.notes: A teacher-approved native format is acceptable. Give the starter in its editable format; no export is needed to demonstrate editing.

slides.title: Check how the audience will see it
body: Preview the deck. Look for small text, overlaps, missing labels and the wrong order.
Read the chart caption and takeaway together.
If available, add concise alternative text using the same data summary.
slides.prompt: What does a useful chart description need?
slides.answer: That the data is fictional, the activity counts and the point it supports.
slides.notes: Do not make an exact menu claim for alternative text. A factual visible caption is core; alternate-text entry is supported where the software permits it.

slides.title: Feedback that points to a change
body: A: “It is bad.”
B: “The chart labels are small; could you enlarge the chart and shorten the caption?”
C: “Make every slide a different style.”
slides.prompt: Which response gives a useful next step?
slides.answer: B identifies an observable issue and a relevant change.
slides.notes: Pupils may use the provided feedback card instead of peer feedback. They can ask an adult to preview privately or explain their choices in writing.

slides.title: Save, reopen and improve
body: Save as GROW_W4_Makers_Club_v1.pptx in the approved task folder.
Reopen the copy, preview it and make one useful improvement.
Record what changed and why; save again.
slides.prompt: Which evidence shows the improvement happened?
slides.answer: The saved file visibly shows the corrected size, wording, order or layout, and the pupil can explain its purpose.
slides.notes: Support: complete one slide at a time with prompts. Standard: create/check four slides. Stretch: explain how a caption, data source and image sizing support the audience.

slides.title: Your choice of review route
body: Show one slide privately to an adult, give a written explanation or choose a partner preview.
No public presentation or online sharing is required.
slides.prompt: Why does your deck use this order?
slides.answer: It introduces the club, explains activities/access and ends with a supported data takeaway.
slides.notes: Assess digital communication and checking, not public-speaking confidence. End with safe saving and closing.

worksheet.title: Build slides that help an audience — practical record

tasks.heading: 1 · Plan the four-slide story
tasks.prompt: Use the complete source cards. Give each slide a clear title and purpose.
items: 1: Makers Club introduction. 2: Activities to try.
3: Ways to join in. 4: Fictional club choices.
My final chart takeaway will be: ___.
tasks.answer: Example takeaway: Model making received the most votes, with 9. An equivalent accurate order/explanation is acceptable if all required information is present.

tasks.heading: 2 · Build and insert the visual
tasks.prompt: Open GROW_W4_Mini_Deck_Starter.pptx. Replace the prompts with the supplied facts.
items: Create four complete slides and keep text readable.
Insert assets/GROW_Club_Votes_Chart.png on the final slide; preserve its proportions.
Add “Fictional Makers Club votes” and a correct takeaway.
Save as GROW_W4_Makers_Club_v1.pptx, or the approved native format.
tasks.answer: Four slides cover introduction, four activities, written/spoken/quiet participation and the chart. The chart retains readable labels and the correct 7/9/3/5 values; no personal information or unsupported claim is added.

tasks.heading: 3 · Check and improve
tasks.prompt: Reopen and preview the saved deck. Choose a private adult, optional partner or written review route.
items: Check: slide order, readability, image proportions, fictional-data label and accurate takeaway.
One improvement I made: ___. It helps because ___.
Feedback option: “The chart labels are small; enlarge it and shorten the caption.”
tasks.answer: A valid improvement changes an observed issue: larger legible chart, shorter accurate text, clear title or corrected order. Pupil explains how the audience benefits; decorative change alone needs a reason.

worksheet.exit_question: Why should an image have a purpose in a slide deck?
worksheet.exit_answer: It should explain or support the information; a relevant readable visual helps the audience understand.

preparation: Check the editable four-slide starter and factual chart PNG open in the available software.
Prepare a private preview route and optional peer feedback; no pupil photograph or internet search is needed.
Demonstrate the local image-insertion and proportional-resizing controls before pupils start.
materials: Presentation software and printed source/check cards

timing.activity: Open starter and establish audience
Plan four slides from source facts
Model concise text and chart insertion/resizing
Build the four-slide deck
Preview, improve and save/reopen
Explain one choice and exit
Save/close and reset

teacher.modelling: Show how two concise activity points preserve all four options. Insert the factual chart, retain proportions and verify label readability. Place a short fictional-data caption where it will be visible; preview the whole slide before calling it finished.
misconceptions: A slide does not need a picture just to fill a space.
Fewer words must still preserve the useful meaning.
Changing an image’s proportions can distort it.
Most votes is not necessarily most people or a majority.
Showing to one adult or explaining in writing is a valid review route.
teacher.support: Use one slide at a time with a printed fact card and accessible input. Offer copied wording or adult scribing of a planned point while observing the learner’s actual digital edit. Allow adult support to locate the chart file.
teacher.stretch: Ask the pupil to justify the slide order, add a concise data description and explain why “most people chose model making” is not supported by 9 of 24 votes.
teacher.fallback: Arrange the four complete source cards into a storyboard and draw a box for the chart with its factual caption. Use the printed vote values to explain the takeaway. Observe insertion/resizing later; paper layout is not a substitute for that practical skill.
teacher.safeguarding: Use only the provided fictional facts and original chart. Do not insert pupil photographs, identifiable information, live profile content or unapproved downloads. No presentation is sent, published or uploaded. Save in the approved school folder.
teacher.assessment: Observe a completed four-slide file, purposeful image insertion with proportions/readability intact, accurate supplied facts and one saved improvement. Record the support used. Public speaking and personal disclosure are not assessment conditions.

resources.title: Makers Club: complete slide facts and check cards
resources.instructions: Use these facts to build four slides. The club and votes are fictional. The chart supplied in the assets folder was created for this pack.
items: Slide 1 · Makers Club. A fictional place to draw, make, code, garden and plan ideas together.
Slide 2 · Activities: drawing; model making; coding; gardening. Use short points that keep all four options.
Slide 3 · Members can offer spoken or written ideas. A quiet idea-sharing option is available. A club adult can help with access needs.
Slide 4 · Fictional vote data: Drawing 7; Model making 9; Coding 3; Gardening 5. Total 24.
Chart image · assets/GROW_Club_Votes_Chart.png. Caption: “Fictional Makers Club votes”. Possible takeaway: “Model making received the most votes: 9.”
Review card A · Can a reader see the title, points, chart labels and fictional-data caption?
Review card B · Is the chart resized without stretching or covering other information?
Review card C · “The chart labels are small. Could you enlarge it and shorten the caption?” Use this as optional feedback.
answers: The supplied facts support the four-slide sequence and the exact 7/9/3/5 chart. Model making leads Drawing by 2 votes.
Nine of 24 is below half, so “most popular option” or “most votes” is accurate; “most people”/“a majority” is not.

lessons.title: Enter, check and explain simple data
lessons.big_question: How can a spreadsheet help us answer a question accurately?
lessons.objective: Enter a supplied fictional dataset, check it with a formula and row comparisons, then create and interpret a labelled chart.
success: I can enter labels and numbers accurately into the intended cells.
I can total and chart the data while keeping labels paired with values.
I can give an accurate comparison and explain a limit of the data.

vocabulary.meaning: A box in a spreadsheet, identified by column and row.
A group of cells, such as B2:B5.
An instruction that calculates a result.
A named group used to organise data.

slides.title: Enter, check and explain simple data
body: Today: build the chart from the fictional club votes used last lesson.
Use supplied counts only. We are not collecting class votes or personal data.
slides.prompt: What is our question?
slides.answer: Which fictional club activity received the most votes, and by how many more than the next option?
slides.notes: Adapted from Week 5 data-handling deck/record. Replaces personal survey/class-size assumptions with complete fictional data and explicit checks. AQA UAS/NC labels remain provisional.

slides.title: A cell has an address
body: Columns use letters; rows use numbers. A1 is column A, row 1.
Put Activity in A1 and Votes in B1. Categories go in A2:A5; numbers go in B2:B5.
A label tells us what a number means.
slides.prompt: What belongs in B3 in the supplied unsorted table?
slides.answer: 9, because row 3 is Model making in this dataset.
slides.notes: Show the selected cell address before entry. The intended order is Drawing, Model making, Coding, Gardening. If the learner sorts later, distinguish the sorted position from the original source position.

slides.title: We do: enter and check one row
body: A2: Drawing. B2: 7.
Read across the row: “Drawing received seven votes.”
Compare both the label and the number with the source card.
slides.prompt: Why read across instead of checking only the number?
slides.answer: A correct number next to the wrong activity still gives incorrect information.
slides.notes: Use number values, not text such as “7 votes”, in the Votes cells. Explain this allows calculation. Provide accessible cell navigation for the available software.

slides.title: You do: complete the four rows
body: Drawing 7; Model making 9; Coding 3; Gardening 5.
Enter all four pairs into A2:B5 in the supplied order.
Check every row against the printed source. These 24 votes are fictional.
slides.prompt: What should you do if your count differs from the card?
slides.answer: Check the intended cell and source, correct the entry, then recheck the row.
slides.notes: Open GROW_W5_Data_Entry_Starter.xlsx. The CSV is a recovery source if entry is inaccessible or time is lost; record that entry was imported rather than independently typed.

slides.title: A formula totals a range
body: Put Total in A7. In B7 enter =SUM(B2:B5).
The result should be 24. Check that the formula includes all four vote cells.
A correct total is useful, but it does not prove every row is correct.
slides.prompt: If Drawing and Model making counts are swapped, would the total still be 24?
slides.answer: Yes. The row labels would be wrong even though the total is unchanged. Check each pair as well.
slides.notes: Single-range SUM syntax checked in Microsoft and LibreOffice primary documentation. If a value is stored as text, it may be ignored; compare the cells rather than guessing the cause.

slides.title: Sort the whole table together
body: Select the complete A1:B5 table, including the headings.
Sort by Votes from largest to smallest, using the heading setting for your software.
Keep each activity attached to its own count. Leave the Total row outside the sort.
slides.prompt: What order should appear after the sort?
slides.answer: Model making 9; Drawing 7; Gardening 5; Coding 3.
slides.notes: Model whole-row sorting so the two columns cannot become detached. If sort controls are inaccessible, use adult support and preserve data accuracy; record the actual skill shown.

slides.title: Make a chart that tells the truth
body: Select A1:B5 and insert a simple bar or column chart. Do not include the Total row.
Title: “Fictional Makers Club choices”. Label the categories and votes; use an axis starting at zero.
Check that each bar matches its category and count.
slides.prompt: Why is Total not another activity bar?
slides.answer: It adds all the activity votes together and is not a separate response option.
slides.notes: Menu placement differs between Excel/Calc. Use the equivalent chart tool. The exact chart orientation may vary; accept any legible bar/column chart with correct values and clear labels.

slides.title: Say only what the data supports
body: Model making received the most votes: 9. Drawing received 7, so the gap is 2.
Nine out of 24 is less than half, so it is not a majority.
The data describes this fictional vote; it does not tell us what everyone likes.
slides.prompt: Improve: “Most people chose model making.”
slides.answer: “Model making was the most popular option in this fictional vote, with 9 of 24 votes.”
slides.notes: Distinguish largest category from majority without requiring percentage calculation. Avoid the source’s “winner” wording when it implies universal preference or exclusion of other choices.

slides.title: Save and check the workbook
body: Save as GROW_W5_Club_Votes_v1.xlsx in the approved folder; an approved native workbook format is also possible.
Reopen and check the four data pairs, formula result and chart.
CSV can store the basic table, but use a workbook format to keep this formula/chart project.
slides.prompt: What checks prove more than a total of 24 alone?
slides.answer: Each labelled data pair matches the source, the range is correct and the chart shows those same values without a Total category.
slides.notes: The expected sum is 24 before and after sorting. Keep a teacher worked workbook and chart fallback distinct from learner-created evidence.

slides.title: Answer with evidence
body: Which activity leads? What is the gap to the next option?
State one thing these numbers cannot tell us.
slides.prompt: Give a complete answer.
slides.answer: Model making leads with 9 votes, 2 more than Drawing. The fictional vote cannot tell us every pupil’s preference or why anyone chose an option.
slides.notes: Accept speaking, pointing to bars or scribed sentences. Save/close before the transition; do not grade a pupil’s personal preference.

worksheet.title: Enter, check and explain simple data — practical record

tasks.heading: 1 · Enter and check the source data
tasks.prompt: Open GROW_W5_Data_Entry_Starter.xlsx. Enter the headings and the complete fictional dataset.
items: A1 Activity; B1 Votes.
A2 Drawing; B2 7. A3 Model making; B3 9.
A4 Coding; B4 3. A5 Gardening; B5 5.
Read each label/count pair back and compare with the source.
tasks.answer: The unsorted table has the exact four pairs 7/9/3/5. Data is fictional and no pupil survey is needed. Entry by import or support should be recorded honestly.

tasks.heading: 2 · Total, sort and chart
tasks.prompt: Use the complete data table, keeping labels and counts together.
items: A7: Total. B7: =SUM(B2:B5). Expected result: 24.
Sort A1:B5 by Votes descending, keeping the heading row and each label/value pair together.
Chart A1:B5 only. Title: Fictional Makers Club choices. Show Activity and Votes labels, with a zero starting point.
Save/reopen GROW_W5_Club_Votes_v1.xlsx or the approved native workbook format.
tasks.answer: After sorting: Model making 9, Drawing 7, Gardening 5, Coding 3. B7 remains 24. Chart contains four categories, not the total. Check row accuracy as well as the total.

tasks.heading: 3 · Interpret and challenge a claim
tasks.prompt: Use the checked table/chart. You can point to the evidence instead of writing long answers.
items: Highest count and activity: ___. Next highest: ___. Difference: ___.
Is 9 of 24 a majority? Explain: ___.
A table swaps Drawing 7 and Model making 9 but still totals 24. Is it accurate? ___.
tasks.answer: Model making 9; Drawing 7; difference 2. No majority: 9 is below half of 24, which is 12. A swapped table is inaccurate despite the unchanged total because the labels/counts no longer match the source.

worksheet.exit_question: Why should we check each row even when the total is right?
worksheet.exit_answer: Different mistakes can leave the total unchanged, such as swapping counts between activities.

preparation: Open the blank-entry starter and teacher worked workbook; check formula/chart compatibility in the school spreadsheet software.
Provide the complete fictional source card and CSV recovery file.
Demonstrate the local whole-table sort and chart tools; ensure the Total row stays outside the selected range.
materials: GROW_W5_Worked_Example.xlsx and factual chart PNG for teacher/recovery use

timing.activity: Access workbook and state the fictional question
Model cell addresses, one row and the SUM range
Enter/check, total, sort and create the chart
Interpret and challenge the majority/total claims
Save/reopen and verify practical record
Exit answer with evidence
Save/close and reset

teacher.modelling: Enter Drawing/7 while saying the cell addresses, then show how a label/count pair carries meaning. Build =SUM(B2:B5), check 24, and demonstrate that swapping two counts would preserve 24 while making the table wrong. Select both columns for sorting and exclude the total from the chart.
misconceptions: A total matching 24 does not prove every row is correct.
Sorting only the numbers can detach them from the labels.
The Total row is not another activity.
Most votes does not mean a majority.
CSV is not the final format for preserving this chart/formula workbook.
teacher.support: Offer a cell-address checklist and one row at a time. Allow accessible input and adult prompting for range selection. If the CSV/worked chart is used, assess checking/interpretation separately and identify unobserved entry/chart skills for later practice.
teacher.stretch: Ask the pupil to explain why a correct total can hide errors, compare largest category with majority, or test a changed count in a temporary copy and predict the new total before checking it.
teacher.fallback: Use printed rows and a calculator or counted marks to total 24, sort cards and sketch a labelled bar chart. Record paper data understanding. Actual spreadsheet entry, formula and chart operations remain to be demonstrated when equipment is available.
teacher.safeguarding: Use only the provided fictional counts. Do not collect pupils’ names, preferences, screen time or other personal data. Keep the workbook in approved storage and do not upload the dataset or chart to a public service.
teacher.assessment: Observe accurate entry, the SUM formula/range, preservation of label/value pairs, a correct chart and an evidence-based comparison. Record which actions were modelled or supported. The teacher worked example is a checking aid, not pupil evidence.

resources.title: Fictional dataset and spreadsheet check cards
resources.instructions: Use these exact practice values. No real survey took place. The rows supply everything needed to enter, total, sort and chart the data.
items: Heading row · A1 = Activity. B1 = Votes.
Row 2 · A2 = Drawing. B2 = 7.
Row 3 · A3 = Model making. B3 = 9.
Row 4 · A4 = Coding. B4 = 3.
Row 5 · A5 = Gardening. B5 = 5.
Total check · A7 = Total. B7 = =SUM(B2:B5). Expected value = 24. Check each row too.
Sort check · Keep A1:B5 together; descending by Votes gives Model making 9, Drawing 7, Gardening 5, Coding 3.
Chart check · Select A1:B5 only; four categories; zero starting axis; title “Fictional Makers Club choices”; clear Activity/Votes labels.
Interpretation check · Model making 9 leads Drawing 7 by 2. Nine of 24 is not more than half. The dataset is fictional and cannot describe everyone’s preferences.
answers: Total 24; highest 9 Model making; second 7 Drawing; difference 2. Half of 24 is 12, so 9 is not a majority.
Swapping counts can keep the total 24 while making the data wrong. Check all label/count pairs, formula range and chart categories.

lessons.title: Online risks and a safer digital footprint
lessons.big_question: How can a person reduce what they reveal and get help with a risky message?
lessons.objective: Recognise risks using fictional examples, edit an offline practice profile to reduce exposure, and explain practical help routes and privacy limits.
success: I can identify a risky request or identifying detail in a fictional example.
I can make purposeful edits that reduce unnecessary exposure.
I can explain why private/deleted content may still be copied and how to seek help.

vocabulary.meaning: Information connected with someone’s online activity, including material others add.
Details that identify someone or reveal information about them.
A deceptive message intended to obtain information or make someone take a risky action.
A control that can limit access to information, with limits.

slides.title: Online risks and a safer digital footprint
body: Today: edit River’s fictional practice profile and respond to fictional message cards.
We will not open personal accounts, share passwords, send messages or publish a profile.
slides.prompt: What can we practise without revealing our own online lives?
slides.answer: Spotting requests, checking details, reducing exposure and choosing a help route using the supplied examples.
slides.notes: Adapted from Week 6 footprint deck/record. ProjectEVOLVE and AQA UAS are source labels only, not claimed endorsement. Replaces personal footprint searches, mandatory positive posting and simple positive/risky binaries.

slides.title: A footprint has different sources
body: A person’s posts and comments can add information. Other people may also post, tag or share material about them.
Services may hold activity data too; not every trace is publicly visible.
Some details reveal more when combined, such as a name, badge and location.
slides.prompt: Can a person have an online footprint without posting their own photo?
slides.answer: Yes. Others may share information about them, and services can hold activity data.
slides.notes: Do not ask learners to search for themselves, show histories or name platforms they use. Distinguish the idea of a trace from a claim that everyone can see all activity.

slides.title: Check the request, not the friendly name
body: A message says, “You have won a device. Send your password now to claim it.”
It could use a friendly name or look official. Good spelling does not prove it is genuine.
Pause and ask an adult; do not follow the message’s link or send secret information.
slides.prompt: Which features make the request concerning?
slides.answer: An unexpected prize, pressure to act and a request for a password. The display name or spelling is not proof of safety.
slides.notes: NCSC guidance confirms authority/urgency tactics and verification through known official routes. The classroom card has no live URL, QR code or credential field.

slides.title: A positive topic can still reveal too much
body: A certificate photo may show a full name or school.
A hobby post can be general, or it can reveal a regular location and time.
A kind comment can still include someone else’s private information.
slides.prompt: Is “it is about an achievement” enough to call a post safe?
slides.answer: No. Check its details, audience and other people’s privacy as well as its positive topic.
slides.notes: Do not promise that removing one label guarantees anonymity. The task is to reduce avoidable exposure; publishing nothing is also a valid choice.

slides.title: We do: reduce a fictional profile’s exposure
body: Open GROW_W6_Fictional_Profile_Starter.docx. Keep River as a fictional display name and the general drawing interest.
Remove the school and live-location fields from this practice copy.
Replace the certificate-photo line with a general text description that contains no identifying details.
slides.prompt: Why is this a useful edit?
slides.answer: It removes information the practice profile does not need and reduces clues that could identify or locate someone.
slides.notes: Bracketed placeholders must never be replaced with real details. This is offline editing, not a real account setting change. Keep the original starter for comparison.

slides.title: Private and deleted are not guarantees
body: Privacy settings can reduce who sees content, but an allowed viewer may copy or share it.
Deleting a post may help remove that copy; screenshots or other copies may remain.
People can still seek help with removal or unwanted sharing. It is not “too late”.
slides.prompt: Improve: “Deleting never helps, because everything is online forever.”
slides.answer: Deleting can help, but it cannot guarantee every copy disappears. Ask for support with unwanted content.
slides.notes: Avoid fatalistic permanence claims, employer scare tactics and blame. Harm is the responsibility of the person causing it, not something a learner deserves because they shared a detail.

slides.title: You do: fix the advice as well as the details
body: Replace “Only friends can ever copy this” with an accurate privacy sentence.
Replace the plan to send a password with a safe pause-and-help response.
Save the offline copy as GROW_W6_River_Profile_Safer_v1.docx.
slides.prompt: What should the password-message response say?
slides.answer: Do not send a password or click the message link. Tell an available trusted adult and verify through the school’s known route if needed.
slides.notes: Accept a teacher-approved native document format. No real report or message is submitted. Adult can read/record the pupil’s reason separately from the digital edits.

slides.title: Pause, get help and use the right route
body: If an online situation worries someone, they can stop interacting and tell a trusted adult.
Adults can help use the platform’s reporting/blocking tools or school IT/safeguarding route.
If a pupil already clicked or shared something, prompt help still matters. They should not be blamed.
slides.prompt: Must someone handle the whole problem alone before telling an adult?
slides.answer: No. Help can be requested immediately, including after a mistake or unwanted sharing.
slides.notes: For online sexual abuse/grooming, staff can use the CEOP reporting route; general bullying or hacking needs the appropriate route. Do not require pupils to collect or forward harmful images as evidence.

slides.title: Check your edited profile and response
body: Task 1: identify the risk and a clue on each card.
Task 2: make and explain edits to River’s offline practice profile.
Task 3: correct an overclaim and choose an available help route.
slides.prompt: What should a final check look for?
slides.answer: No real identifying details; an accurate privacy limit; a safe response to the password request; a named task file that reopens.
slides.notes: Support: select between two edits and demonstrate one replacement. Standard: complete the profile/advice changes. Stretch: explain why a positive topic or known display name alone does not remove risk.

slides.title: A safer next action
body: River already clicked a worrying link and feels embarrassed.
The fictional profile is still an offline classroom document.
slides.prompt: What would you advise River to do next?
slides.answer: Stop interacting with the suspicious content and tell an available adult promptly so the right support can be arranged. It is not a reason to hide the problem.
slides.notes: Identify actual available school adults before dismissal. Respond to any personal disclosure privately through school procedures; do not turn it into class discussion.

worksheet.title: Online risks and a safer digital footprint — practical record

tasks.heading: 1 · Recognise the risk and clue
tasks.prompt: Read the fictional cards. Identify a concern and one useful next step.
items: A: “Free device! Send your password now.”
B: A certificate image shows a full name and school.
C: A group piles on one person with hurtful messages.
tasks.answer: A: deceptive/pressuring credential request; do not reply or follow its link, ask an adult. B: identifying details despite positive content; remove details or choose not to share. C: harmful behaviour; do not join/forward, get adult support and appropriate reporting help.

tasks.heading: 2 · Edit River’s practice profile
tasks.prompt: Open GROW_W6_Fictional_Profile_Starter.docx. Make a safer offline copy; never fill the brackets with real information.
items: Keep River’s fictional display name and general interest. Remove school and live-location fields.
Replace the certificate-photo line with a general non-identifying text description.
Correct the claim that a private account prevents all copying.
Replace the plan to send a password with a safe adult-help response. Save/reopen GROW_W6_River_Profile_Safer_v1.docx.
tasks.answer: A suitable copy keeps only general fictional interests, removes identifying/location fields, states that allowed viewers may still copy content, and advises not replying/clicking/sending passwords while seeking adult help. Equivalent clear wording is valid.

tasks.heading: 3 · Explain a limit and get support
tasks.prompt: Use River’s fictional situation, not a personal online history.
items: Improve: “If I delete something, nobody can ever see a copy again.”
River’s first adult is unavailable. A pastoral adult and the school safeguarding lead are available. What can River do?
One practical edit I made and why it matters: ___.
tasks.answer: Deletion can help but copies/screenshots may remain. River can approach an available pastoral/safeguarding adult and say if help is urgent. Example edit: remove live location because the profile does not need to reveal where River is.

worksheet.exit_question: Why is a private account not a promise that content cannot spread?
worksheet.exit_answer: Someone with access may copy or share it; privacy controls reduce exposure but have limits.

preparation: Read the fictional profile and cards; confirm there are no active URLs, account forms or real identifying details.
Identify actual school IT, pastoral and safeguarding help routes.
Check the word processor and writable starter copy; explain that all changes remain offline classroom practice.
materials: School-managed word processor and practical record

timing.activity: Set fictional-only boundaries and help route
Teach footprint sources and request-based risk clues
Model an exposure edit and privacy correction
Edit/save/reopen the practice profile
Discuss cards and accurate help responses

teacher.modelling: Think aloud: “A certificate celebrates something, but it may reveal a name and school. I can choose a general description without those details.” Replace the private-account overclaim and show how a safe response focuses on an adult-help route, not on replying to the message.
misconceptions: A positive topic does not guarantee a post reveals no sensitive details.
A familiar display name or good spelling does not prove a message is genuine.
Not every trace is publicly visible.
Privacy/deletion can help but cannot guarantee control of all copies.
There is no duty to publish positive content or investigate harm alone.
teacher.support: Use one short card at a time with two possible next actions. Read text aloud and offer supported selection/replacement in the document. Allow an adult to scribe explanations without requiring personal examples.
teacher.stretch: Ask the pupil to identify combined clues in an apparently harmless post, explain why a certificate may be identifying, or compare a realistic privacy statement with an absolute promise.
teacher.fallback: Use the full printed profile card to cross out unnecessary fields and rewrite the two unsafe claims. Record risk reasoning and planned edits; observe digital editing separately later. No internet connection is needed.
teacher.safeguarding: No real accounts, passwords, histories, photos, messages or personal details are inspected or collected. Do not forward harmful content or ask pupils to retrieve it. If a concern is disclosed, listen privately, do not promise secrecy, record/report through school safeguarding procedures and involve appropriate staff. Seek emergency help for immediate danger.
teacher.assessment: Check identification of risk using a specific clue, purposeful deletion/replacement in the practice copy, an accurate privacy/deletion limit and a realistic help route. Assess understanding and demonstrated edits, not a pupil’s own online experiences or choices.

resources.title: Fictional profile and risk-response cards
resources.instructions: All examples are classroom simulations. Read or edit the complete text; do not substitute real names, locations, accounts or passwords.

Profile source · Photo caption: My certificate showing my full name and school. Privacy claim: Only friends can ever copy this because my account is private.
Profile source · Draft message: Someone offered a free device if I send my password. I will reply.
Risk card A · An unexpected message offers a free device and demands a password immediately. It has no clickable link in this exercise.
Risk card B · A certificate photo reveals a full name and school, even though the topic is an achievement.
Risk card C · A group posts hurtful messages about one person. A bystander is asked to forward them.
Claim check · “Deleting means every copy is gone.” “Private means nobody can copy.” Both need correcting.
Help options · Stop interacting; tell an available trusted adult; ask staff about school IT/safeguarding or platform report/block routes. Do not investigate or forward harmful content.
answers: Keep fictional River/general interests; remove school/live-location fields and replace the certificate line with a non-identifying general statement.
Private settings may limit access but viewers can copy. Deleting can help, but copies can remain. Do not send passwords or follow the suspicious message; seek help.
C: do not join or forward the harm; seek adult support. A pupil is not to blame for another person’s harmful behaviour and can seek help after a mistake.

lessons.objective: Create a document or presentation about fictional River, combining purposeful formatting, a checked chart, accurate data reasoning and safer online choices.

I can show purposeful editing, a readable chart and an accurate data comparison.
I can explain safer choices, reopen the saved project and improve one part.
